source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. V (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: Et factum est, postquam percussit Alexander Philippi Macedo
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: Now it came to pass, after that Alexander the son of Philip the Macedonian

paras.t: Gesta Machabæorum multis annis post reditum a captivitate Babylonica contigerunt. Historia quippe Tobiæ præcessit satis diu historiam Judith, historia quoque Judith historiam Esther. Sed et historia Esther, historiam Machabæorum: quod, prolixitatem vitans, declarare non prosequor; sed ad Josephum atque Scholasticam historiam mitto lectorem. Ponitur autem in exordio hujus libri aliquid de Alexandro Magno, et de divisione monarchiæ suæ, ut sic ordinate ad gesta deveniatur Machabæorum, imo ad notificationem providentiæ, justitiæ, misericordiæ et beneficentiæ Dei circa populum Judæorum, durante adhuc cursu veteris Testamenti. Non est autem hic liber in canone: tamen ab Ecclesia tanquam verus receptus est.
paras.en: The deeds of the Machabees took place many years after the return from the Babylonian captivity. For the history of Tobias came a good while before the history of Judith, and the history of Judith before that of Esther; and the history of Esther, too, before that of the Machabees. This I do not set out to show, so as to avoid length; but I send the reader to Josephus [the margin cites Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book XI] and to the Scholastic History [the Historia scholastica of Peter Comestor, whom Denis calls 'the Master in the Histories']. Now at the opening of this book something is set down about Alexander the Great and the division of his monarchy, so that the account may come in due order to the deeds of the Machabees, or rather to the making known of the providence, justice, mercy and kindness of God towards the people of the Jews while the course of the Old Testament was still running. This book is not in the canon; yet it has been received by the Church as true [Denis means the Hebrew canon, following Jerome; the Council of Trent later defined both books of Machabees as canonical].

paras.t: Et factum est. Cur a conjunctione hac, et, incipit, quum nihil præmiserit, inter quæ mediet et connectat? Et respondendum, quod incipit sic, ad innuendum quod multa omittat gesta historica, quæ mente consideravit, sed stilo non expressit. Ad ea ergo quæ mente intuebatur, ista conjungens quæ scripsit, sic incipit: Et factum est. Sic et Ezechiel et Jonas suos exorsi sunt libros.
paras.en: [[1:1|Now it came to pass|Et factum est]] [the Latin is *Et factum est*, 'And it came to pass'; the Douay-Rheims renders the *Et* as 'Now']. Why does he begin with this conjunction, *and*, when he has set down nothing before it, between which and what follows it might stand and join them? It must be answered that he begins so in order to hint that he leaves out many deeds of the history, which he considered in his mind but did not express with his pen. Joining, then, what he wrote to the things he was beholding in his mind, he begins thus: [[1:1|Now it came to pass|Et factum est]]. So too Ezechiel and Jonas began their books.

paras.t: Postquam percussit Alexander Philippi filius, Macedo, id est de Macedonia provincia Græciæ oriundus, in qua et primo regnavit, defuncto rege Philippo, cujus filius putativus fuit Alexander: quia revera (ut ejus testatur historia) fuit filius Nectanabis regis Ægypti, qui timore adversariorum suorum, mutato habitu, fugit et exivit Ægyptum, atque ad uxorem Philippi regis Macedonum veniens, ad mulieris illius familiaritatem receptus est, et cum ea concumbens, ex eadem genuit Alexandrum per adulterium. Philippus autem rex putavit se verum Alexandri patrem. Unde et nato Alexandro, Aristoteli scripsit: Natus est mihi filius, et magis regratior diis, quia natus est tuis temporibus, quam quia natus est, quoniam a te eum informandum confido.
paras.en: [[1:1|after that Alexander the son of Philip the Macedonian|Postquam percussit Alexander Philippi filius, Macedo]] had overthrown Darius: *the Macedonian*, that is, sprung from Macedonia, a province of Greece, in which he also first reigned after the death of King Philip, whose reputed son Alexander was. For in truth (as his history testifies) he was the son of Nectanabis, king of Egypt, who for fear of his enemies changed his dress, fled and left Egypt, and coming to the wife of Philip king of the Macedonians, was received into that woman's familiarity; and lying with her, he begot Alexander of her in adultery. But King Philip thought himself Alexander's true father. Hence too, when Alexander was born, he wrote to Aristotle: A son is born to me, and I give more thanks to the gods that he was born in your times than that he was born at all, since I trust that he will be formed by you.

paras.t: Præterea, Alexander dicitur Darium percussisse, non quod manu propria, aut per suum exercitum occiderit illum, sed quoniam fugavit ipsum in bello. Quumque fugiens Darius, pervenisset in suum palatium, a duobus de suis principibus est occisus. Alexander autem insequens eum, reperit eum adhuc semivivum, et multum condoluit ei. Et tunc Darius utiliter admonuit Alexandrum, ne ex victoriis superbiret, et inter cetera ordinavit, ut filiam suam Alexander duceret conjugem: quod et factum est.
paras.en: Further, Alexander is said to have overthrown Darius [*percussisse*, literally 'struck'], not because he killed him with his own hand or through his army, but because he put him to flight in battle. And when Darius in his flight had reached his palace, he was slain by two of his own princes. But Alexander, pursuing him, found him still half alive, and grieved much for him. And then Darius gave Alexander the useful warning not to grow proud of his victories, and among other things arranged that Alexander should take his daughter to wife: which was done.

paras.t: Sed quæri potest, quis fuerit Darius iste. Ad quod quidam respondet, quod secundum Hebræos fuit filius Assueri ac Esther: quod stare non potest; nec omnes Hebræi hoc dicunt. Imo (ut refert ille) Hebræi dicunt Darium illum qui post Cyrum regem renovavit et dedit Judæis licentiam ædificandi templum et urbem Jerusalem. Fuit Darius ille filius Assueri et Esther, ita quod favorabilis fuit Judæis, quia ex matre Hebræa exstitit natus. Et tamen nec hoc verum est; et certum est quod temporibus illius Darii nondum erat Alexander hic genitus. Nempe illi Dario successit in regnum filius ejus Artaxerxes, sub quo Esdras et postea Nehemias venerunt in Jerusalem: quod et Josephus attestatur, quamvis alia nomina ponat. Post Artaxerxem regnavit Xerxes, quem Josephus dicit fuisse Assuerum. Alii vero, quos Magister in historiis sequitur, affirmant quod post Artaxerxem regnavit Xerxes duobus mensibus; post Xerxem, Sogdianus mensibus septem; post Sogdianum, Darius cognomento Nothus; post Darium Nothum, Artaxerxes cognomento Mnemon, quem ut in Scholastica fertur historia, dicunt Hebræi Assuerum fuisse; post quem regnavit Artaxerxes, qui dictus est Ochus; post Ochum, Arsamus; post Arsamum, filius ejus Darius, quem Alexander devicit.
paras.en: But it may be asked who this Darius was. To which a certain writer answers that according to the Hebrews he was the son of Assuerus and Esther: which cannot stand; nor do all the Hebrews say so. Rather (as he reports) the Hebrews say this of the Darius who after King Cyrus renewed the decree and gave the Jews leave to build the temple and the city of Jerusalem[[1 Esd 6:3||]]: that Darius was the son of Assuerus and Esther, and so was favourable to the Jews, being born of a Hebrew mother. And yet neither is this true; and it is certain that in the times of that Darius this Alexander was not yet born. For that Darius was succeeded in the kingdom by his son Artaxerxes, under whom Esdras[[1 Esd 7:1||]] and afterwards Nehemias[[2 Esd 2:1||]] came to Jerusalem: which Josephus too attests, though he gives other names. After Artaxerxes reigned Xerxes, who Josephus says was Assuerus. But others, whom the Master in the Histories follows, affirm that after Artaxerxes Xerxes reigned two months; after Xerxes, Sogdianus seven months; after Sogdianus, Darius surnamed Nothus; after Darius Nothus, Artaxerxes surnamed Mnemon, who, as is related in the Scholastic History, the Hebrews say was Assuerus; after him reigned Artaxerxes, who was called Ochus; after Ochus, Arsamus; after Arsamus, his son Darius, whom Alexander overcame.

paras.t: Qui Alexander primus regnavit in Græcia, id est, primus fuit monarcha Græcorum, et in tota Græcia, totoque oriente regnavit et imperavit, quoniam monarchiam Persarum destruxit, et transtulit monarchiam ad Græcos: designatus in visione Danielis per hircum caprarum, qui terram non tetigit, quia celerrime omnia devastando pertransiit. Egressus de terra Cethim: locus est Græciæ; non solitudinis, unde habetur in Numeris, Morabatur eo tempore Israel in Cethim. Darium regem Persarum et Medorum. A tempore enim Cyri regis fuerunt illa regna in uno rege unita, defuncto avunculo Cyri, Dario nomine, qui cum Cyro Babylonem destruxit.
paras.en: This Alexander [[1:1|who first reigned in Greece|primus regnavit in Græcia]]: that is, he was the first monarch of the Greeks, and reigned and ruled in all Greece and in the whole East, since he destroyed the monarchy of the Persians and transferred the monarchy to the Greeks. He was signified in the vision of Daniel by the he goat[[Dan 8:21||]], which [[Dan 8:5|touched not the ground|terram non tetigit]], because he passed through most swiftly, laying all waste. [[1:1|coming out of the land of Cethim|Egressus de terra Cethim]]: this is a place of Greece; not the place in the wilderness, of which we have in Numbers: [[Num 25:1|Israel at that time abode in Settim|Morabatur eo tempore Israel in Cethim]] [Denis's text reads *Cethim* here; the editors note that the Vulgate has *Settim*, the place of that name in the wilderness]. [[1:1|Darius, king of the Persians and Medes|Darium regem Persarum et Medorum]]: for from the time of King Cyrus those kingdoms were united under one king, after the death of Cyrus's uncle, named Darius, who with Cyrus destroyed Babylon.

paras.t: Constituit prælia. Nam Dario isto dejecto, perrexit ad Indiam contra Porum regem Indorum; et in via præliatus est contra alios multos quos superavit. Unde subjungitur: et omnium obtinuit munitiones, hoc est loca munita, videlicet castra, fortalitia, oppida (inquam) omnium repugnantium sibi. Et siluit terra in conspectu ejus, id est, habitantes in terra, contra eum rebellare aut clamare non præsumpserunt, præsertim postquam Porum regem Indorum devicit.
paras.en: [[1:2|He fought many battles|Constituit prælia]]. For when this Darius had been cast down, he went on to India against Porus king of the Indians; and on the way he fought against many others, whom he overcame. Hence it is added: [[1:2|and took the strong holds of all|et omnium obtinuit munitiones]], that is, fortified places, namely camps, strongholds, towns (I say) of all who resisted him. [[1:3|and the earth was quiet before him|Et siluit terra in conspectu ejus]] [*siluit*, literally 'was silent']: that is, the dwellers on the earth did not presume to rebel or cry out against him, especially after he overcame Porus king of the Indians.

paras.t: Et congregavit virtutem, id est robur bellicum, et exercitum fortem nimis. Nam primo habuit parvum exercitum, comparative loquendo; sed ex gentibus quas debellavit, conjunxit sibi auxiliarios multos et elegantes, quemadmodum de Holoferne narratur: De universis urbibus assumpsit sibi auxiliarios viros fortes et electos ad prælium. Et præsertim Persæ et Medi ab Alexandro devicti, facti sunt ei multum fideles, sicut et ipse exhibuit eis se clementem. Et regnum Persarum commisit avunculo Darii; duos quoque principes qui Darium vulneraverunt usque ad mortem, occidit. Et pertransiit usque ad fines terræ. Transivit enim per maximam et horribilem Indiæ eremum, in qua multa pericula toleravit, et tandem devenit ad arbores solis et lunæ, ubi responsum accepit de sua morte: sicque ad fines terræ deveniens versus orientem, intravit Oceanum remotius quam Hercules ante eum, et statuit illic columnas ultra columnas ab Hercule positas. Et exaltatus est potestate, honore atque latissima jurisdictione, et elevatum est cor ejus, per superbiam et ambitionem; tamen audita responsione quod cito moreretur, humiliavit cor suum in multis. Et obtinuit regiones gentium et tyrannos; et facti sunt illi in tributum, hoc est tributarii, hi quos vicit.
paras.en: [[1:4|And he gathered a power|Et congregavit virtutem]], that is, warlike strength, [[1:4|and a very strong army|et exercitum fortem nimis]]. For at first he had a small army, comparatively speaking; but from the nations he conquered he joined to himself many choice auxiliaries, as is told of Holofernes: [[Jdt 3:8|And from all the cities he took auxiliaries valiant men, and chosen for war|De universis urbibus assumpsit sibi auxiliarios viros fortes et electos ad prælium]]. And especially the Persians and Medes, conquered by Alexander, became very faithful to him, as he too showed himself merciful to them. And he entrusted the kingdom of the Persians to the uncle of Darius; and the two princes who had wounded Darius to death, he slew. [[1:3|And he went through even to the ends of the earth|Et pertransiit usque ad fines terræ]]. For he passed through the very great and dreadful desert of India, in which he endured many dangers, and at last came to the trees of the sun and the moon, where he received an answer about his death; and so, coming to the ends of the earth towards the east, he entered the Ocean further than Hercules before him, and set up there pillars beyond the pillars set up by Hercules. And he [[1:4|was exalted|Et exaltatus est]] in power, honour and the widest jurisdiction [Denis reads *exaltatus est*, 'he was exalted', where the Vulgate has *exaltatum est*, said of his heart], [[1:4|and his heart was exalted and lifted up|et elevatum est cor ejus]] through pride and ambition; yet, having heard the answer that he would soon die, he humbled his heart in many things. [[1:5|And he subdued countries of nations, and princes|Et obtinuit regiones gentium et tyrannos]]; [[1:5|and they became tributaries to him|et facti sunt illi in tributum]], that is, those whom he conquered became tributaries.

paras.t: Et post hæc decidit in lectum, et cognovit quia moreretur. Fuit enim infectus a Jolo suo pincerna, cui antea dederat alapam. Et vocavit pueros suos nobiles, id est collegas, qui secum erant nutriti a juventute sua, et divisit illis regnum suum, id est imperium, non unicum regnum, dum adhuc viveret. Fertur tamen in sua legenda, quod ex conjuge sua filia Darii genuit filium, qui adhuc erat infantulus. Divisit autem regnum suum seu monarchiam in duodecim partes, nolens quod aliquis ei par postea legeretur; sed dispositio illa fuit cassata, quoniam aliis abjectis, non nisi quatuor successerunt eidem, quemadmodum a Daniele fuit prædictum. Denique sumpto veneno in Babylone Ægypti, mox loquelam amisit, et extremam suam voluntatem scripto insinuavit. Jolus autem et frater ejus Cassander, etiam uxorem Alexandri et filium ejus infantulum peremerunt. Et regnavit Alexander annis duodecim, ex quibus (ut legitur) imperavit annis sex aut septem in pace; et vixit annis triginta duobus; et mortuus est.
paras.en: [[1:6|And after these things, he fell down upon his bed, and knew that he should die.|Et post hæc decidit in lectum, et cognovit quia moreretur]] For he had been poisoned by Jolus his cupbearer, whom he had earlier struck on the cheek. [[1:7|And he called his servants, the nobles|Et vocavit pueros suos nobiles]], that is, his companions, [[1:7|that were brought up with him from his youth|qui secum erant nutriti a juventute sua]], [[1:7|and he divided his kingdom among them|et divisit illis regnum suum]], that is, his empire, not a single kingdom, [[1:7|while he was yet alive|dum adhuc viveret]]. It is related, however, in his legend, that by his wife, the daughter of Darius, he begot a son, who was still a little infant. Now he divided his kingdom or monarchy into twelve parts, not wishing that anyone should afterwards be chosen as his equal; but that arrangement was made void, since the others were thrust aside and only four succeeded him, as had been foretold by Daniel[[Dan 8:8||]][[Dan 8:22||]]. At length, having taken poison in Babylon of Egypt [so the text; Alexander died at Babylon on the Euphrates], he soon lost his speech, and made his last will known in writing. And Jolus and his brother Cassander killed Alexander's wife too, and his infant son. [[1:8|And Alexander reigned twelve years|Et regnavit Alexander annis duodecim]], of which (as we read) he ruled six or seven years in peace; and he lived thirty-two years; [[1:8|and he died|et mortuus est]].

paras.t: Et obtinuerunt pueri ejus, id est sodales præfati, regnum, unusquisque in loco suo sibi deputato: quod tamen de quatuor principalibus pueris et successoribus ejus accipitur. Et imposuerunt sibi omnes diademata post mortem ejus; et multiplicata sunt mala pœnæ et culpæ in terra: quoniam successores Alexandri contra se invicem acerrime et implacabiliter pugnaverunt, et quidam eorum (sicut infra habetur) vehementissime oppresserunt Israeliticum populum, præsertim reges Syriæ et Ægypti, maxime vero Antiochus Nobilis, de quo subditur.
paras.en: [[1:9|And his servants|Et obtinuerunt pueri ejus]], that is, the aforesaid companions, [[1:9|made themselves kings, every one in his place|regnum, unusquisque in loco suo]] assigned to him: which, however, is understood of four chief servants and successors of his. [[1:10|And they all put crowns upon themselves after his death|Et imposuerunt sibi omnes diademata post mortem ejus]]; [[1:10|and evils were multiplied|et multiplicata sunt mala]], evils of punishment and of guilt, [[1:10|in the earth|in terra]]: since the successors of Alexander fought against one another most fiercely and implacably, and some of them (as is told below) most grievously oppressed the people of Israel, especially the kings of Syria and of Egypt, but above all Antiochus the Noble, of whom it follows:

paras.t: Et exiit ex illis radix peccati Antiochus Illustris, id est, ex semine regum illorum natus est Antiochus, dictus Illustris, quoniam acer et strenuus fuit in bellis. Et primo præbuit se cunctis benignum ac liberalem, propter quod vocaverunt eum Epiphanem, id est illustrem: qui factus rex, vitiositatem suam, quam diu absconderat, cœpit ostendere; et tam sceleratissimus fuit, ut merito appelletur radix peccati, quoniam per se et per subditos suos fecit innumerabilia et crudelissima mala, præsertim in populum Judæorum, imo et in consanguineos suos reges Ægypti; fuitque valde dolosus. Filius Antiochi regis Syriæ, qui vocatur Antiochus Major: de quo inter multa recitat Josephus, quod fuit Judæis valde fidelis et pius, sicut et infra secundo tangitur libro; qui, Antiochus Illustris, fuerat Romæ obses, id est obstagius. Quum enim pater ejus infestaret Ægyptum, missi sunt duo legati Romanorum, qui compulerunt eum inde recedere, et filium ejus seniorem Seleucum, pro majori securitate, obsidem acceperunt. Antiochus vero sciens crudelitatem filii sui Antiochi, rogavit ut illum pro fratre acciperent obsidem: quod et fecerunt, ut Josephus narrat duodecimo libro Antiquitatum. Et regnavit in anno centesimo tricesimo septimo regni Græcorum: incipiendo hanc numerationem annorum a monarchia Græcorum, hoc est a regno monarchico quod incipit ab Alexandro; atque in ejus morte fuit monarchia illa finita. Et cito post hoc cœperunt Romani ad monarchiam adspirare: quam et post multa et magna bella obtinuerunt; et major fuit eorum monarchia quam Alexandri, nec adhuc in toto destructa.
paras.en: [[1:11|And there came out of them a wicked root, Antiochus the Illustrious|Et exiit ex illis radix peccati Antiochus Illustris]] [Denis reads *radix peccati*, 'a root of sin', where the Vulgate has *radix peccatrix*, 'a wicked root']: that is, of the seed of those kings was born Antiochus, called the Illustrious because he was keen and vigorous in war. And at first he showed himself kind and generous to all, for which reason they called him Epiphanes, that is, illustrious; but once made king, he began to show his viciousness, which he had long hidden; and he was so very wicked that he is rightly called a root of sin, since by himself and by his subjects he did numberless and most cruel evils, especially against the people of the Jews, and indeed against his own kinsmen, the kings of Egypt; and he was very deceitful. [[1:11|the son of king Antiochus|Filius Antiochi regis]] of Syria, who is called Antiochus the Great: of whom Josephus relates among many things that he was very faithful and kind to the Jews, as is also touched on below in the second book. He, Antiochus the Illustrious, [[1:11|had been a hostage at Rome|fuerat Romæ obses]], that is, a pledge. For when his father was harassing Egypt, two legates of the Romans were sent, who forced him to withdraw from there, and took his elder son Seleucus as a hostage for greater security. But Antiochus, knowing the cruelty of his son Antiochus, asked that they take him as hostage in place of his brother: which they did, as Josephus relates in the twelfth book of the Antiquities. [[1:11|and he reigned in the hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks|Et regnavit in anno centesimo tricesimo septimo regni Græcorum]]: beginning this reckoning of years from the monarchy of the Greeks, that is, from the monarchical kingdom which begins with Alexander; and at his death that monarchy came to an end. And soon after this the Romans began to aspire to monarchy: which they obtained after many great wars; and their monarchy was greater than Alexander's, and is not yet wholly destroyed.

paras.t: In diebus illis exierunt ex Israel filii iniqui, et suaserunt multis, dicentes: Eamus et disponamus testamentum, hoc est fœdus amicitiæ et ritum religionis, cum gentibus quæ circa nos sunt, id est cum gentilibus idololatris; quia ex quo recessimus ab eis per disparem cultum et resistentiam, invenerunt nos multa mala pœnalia, id est, diversas et duras adversitates et persecutiones sumus perpessi. Et bonus visus est sermo in oculis eorum: id est, judicaverunt sic esse, non attendentes quod multæ sint tribulationes justorum, quos Deus exercet et purgat per impios; nec etiam considerantes, quod juxta Prophetarum oracula, tam regnum Juda quam regnum Israel fuerunt destructa, potissime propter idololatriæ ritum, et quod tempore judicum fuerunt hostibus traditi propter deorum culturam. Impii isti fuerunt similes Judæis nequissimis, qui leguntur ad Jeremiam dixisse: Verbum quod locutus es ad nos in nomine Domini, non audiemus ex te; sed faciemus omne verbum quod egredietur de ore nostro, ut sacrificemus reginæ cœli, id est lunæ, sicut fecimus et saturati sumus, malumque non vidimus. Ex eo autem tempore quo cessavimus reginæ cœli sacrificare, indigemus omnibus, et gladio et fame consumpti sumus. Quorum perfidiam et errorem reprobat ibi Jeremias.
paras.en: [[1:12|In those days there went out of Israel wicked men, and they persuaded many, saying: Let us go and make a covenant|In diebus illis exierunt ex Israel filii iniqui, et suaserunt multis, dicentes: Eamus et disponamus testamentum]], that is, a league of friendship and a rite of religion, [[1:12|with the heathens that are round about us|cum gentibus quæ circa nos sunt]], that is, with the idolatrous Gentiles; [[1:12|for since we departed from them|quia ex quo recessimus ab eis]] by a different worship and by resistance, [[1:12|many evils have befallen us|invenerunt nos multa mala]], evils of punishment: that is, we have suffered various and hard adversities and persecutions. [[1:13|And the word seemed good in their eyes|Et bonus visus est sermo in oculis eorum]]: that is, they judged it to be so, not heeding that [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ sint tribulationes justorum]], whom God exercises and purges by the wicked; nor yet considering that, according to the oracles of the Prophets, both the kingdom of Juda and the kingdom of Israel were destroyed chiefly for the rite of idolatry[[Ezech 16:1||]][[Ezech 23:1||]] [the margin, partly illegible, seems to give Ezech. xvi and xxiii], and that in the time of the judges they were delivered to their enemies for the worship of gods[[Judg 2:14||]] [the margin gives Judges *passim*]. These wicked men were like the most wicked Jews who, we read, said to Jeremias: [[Jer 44:16|As for the word which thou hast spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not hearken to thee|Verbum quod locutus es ad nos in nomine Domini, non audiemus ex te]]; [[Jer 44:17|But we will certainly do every word that shall proceed out of our own mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven|sed faciemus omne verbum quod egredietur de ore nostro, ut sacrificemus reginæ cœli]], that is, to the moon, as we did, and [[Jer 44:17|we were filled|saturati sumus]], [[Jer 44:17|and we saw no evil|malumque non vidimus]]. [[Jer 44:18|But since we left off to offer sacrifice to the queen of heaven|Ex eo autem tempore quo cessavimus reginæ cœli sacrificare]], [[Jer 44:18|we have wanted all things, and have been consumed by the sword, and by famine|indigemus omnibus, et gladio et fame consumpti sumus]]. Their faithlessness and error Jeremias there condemns[[Jer 44:20||]].

paras.t: Et destinaverunt aliqui de populo, hoc est, proposuerunt sic agere, vel miserunt nuntios, et abierunt quidam ex parte illorum ad regem Antiochum; et dedit illis potestatem ut facerent justitias gentium, id est opera idololatriæ, quæ gentiles justa esse putabant. Et ædificaverunt gymnasium in Jerosolymis. Gymnasium proprie dicitur locus, in quo homines exercentur ad luctam corporalem, et cursorum probatur velocitas. Hinc transfertur ad significandum scholas, locumque studii, in quo est exercitatio animi ad opponendum ac respondendum: et ita hic sumitur pro schola, in qua docentur statuta et ritus gentilium. Et fecerunt sibi, hoc est, in se et in suis esse permiserunt, præputia, non circumcidendo filios suos, et ritu præputiatorum vivebant; atque, ut Josephus scribit, fecerunt circumcisioni suæ quædam velamina, ne in denudatione viderentur Græcis dissimiles. Nempe in sacris Priapi incedebant totaliter nudi, sicut et feminæ in sacris Veneris. Et recesserunt a testamento sancto, id est ab observantia legis Mosaicæ; et juncti sunt nationibus, id est gentilibus, quos Judæi quasi parvipendendo, propter eorum incredulitatem, communi nomine nationes vocabant. Unde est illud in Psalmo: Dicite in nationibus, quia Dominus regnavit. Et venundati sunt, hoc est, intuitu commodi temporalis se ipsos tradiderunt, et quasi vendiderunt diabolo per vitiosum consensum, ut facerent malum. Sic tertio libro Regum Elias ait ad Achab: Venundatus es ut faceres malum in conspectu Domini.
paras.en: [[1:14|And some of the people determined|Et destinaverunt aliqui de populo]]: that is, they purposed to act so, or they sent messengers; [[1:14|and went|et abierunt]], some on their behalf, [[1:14|to the king|ad regem]] Antiochus; [[1:14|and he gave them license to do after the ordinances of the heathens|et dedit illis potestatem ut facerent justitias gentium]], that is, the works of idolatry, which the Gentiles thought just [the Latin *justitias*, 'justices', is what the Douay-Rheims renders 'ordinances'; hence Denis's gloss]. [[1:15|And they built a place of exercise in Jerusalem|Et ædificaverunt gymnasium in Jerosolymis]]. A gymnasium [the Douay-Rheims's 'place of exercise'] is properly a place in which men are exercised in bodily wrestling and the speed of runners is tried. From there the word is carried over to signify schools and a place of study, in which there is exercise of the mind in objecting and answering: and so here it is taken for a school in which the statutes and rites of the Gentiles are taught. [[1:16|And they made themselves|Et fecerunt sibi]], that is, they allowed to be in themselves and in their own, [[1:16|prepuces|præputia]], by not circumcising their sons, and they lived by the rite of the uncircumcised; and, as Josephus writes, they made certain coverings for their circumcision, so as not to be seen, when stripped, to be unlike the Greeks. For in the rites of Priapus they went about wholly naked, as did the women in the rites of Venus. [[1:16|and departed from the holy covenant|Et recesserunt a testamento sancto]], that is, from the observance of the Mosaic law; [[1:16|and joined themselves to the heathens|et juncti sunt nationibus]], that is, to the Gentiles, whom the Jews, as though making little of them on account of their unbelief, called by the common name of *nations*. Hence that saying in the Psalm [Denis reads *in nationibus*, 'among the nations', where the Vulgate has *in gentibus*]: [[Ps 95:10|Say ye among the Gentiles, the Lord hath reigned|Dicite in nationibus, quia Dominus regnavit]]. [[1:16|and were sold|Et venundati sunt]]: that is, with an eye to temporal advantage they handed themselves over, and as it were sold themselves to the devil by sinful consent, [[1:16|to do evil|ut facerent malum]]. So in the third book of Kings Elias says to Achab: [[3 Kings 21:20|thou art sold, to do evil in the sight of the Lord|Venundatus es ut faceres malum in conspectu Domini]].

paras.t: Denique, sicut in Scholastica fertur historia: Causa tanti flagitii fuit Onias pontifex, duos habens fratres contendentes pro pontificatu: qui ut placerent Antiocho, petierunt ut liceret eis facere gymnasium in Jerusalem, et ad idololatriam declinare. Et vocabatur unus eorum Jesus, alter Joannes. Verum ad placendum impio regi, imposuerunt sibi gentilia nomina, ita quod Jesus vocavit se Jasonem, Joannes Menelaum: de quibus infra in secundo libro habetur.
paras.en: Moreover, as is related in the Scholastic History: The occasion of so great a crime was the high priest Onias, who had two brothers contending for the high priesthood; these, to please Antiochus, asked that they might be allowed to make a gymnasium in Jerusalem and to turn aside to idolatry. And one of them was called Jesus, the other John. But to please the wicked king they took Gentile names, so that Jesus called himself Jason, and John Menelaus: of whom we read below in the second book[[2 Mach 4:7||]][[2 Mach 4:24||]] [the margin's numerals are unclear: apparently 2 Mach. iv].

paras.t: Et paratum est, id est ad obediendum dispositum, regnum in conspectu Antiochi. Quum enim adhuc Romæ exsistens, percepisset patrem suum obiisse, et sciret fratris sui inertiam, clam, vel (ut aliqui dicunt) de senatorum consensu, recessit a Roma, et venit in Syriam, ac mortuo fratre suo, in regem susceptus est. Et cœpit regnare in terra Ægypti, ut regnaret super duo regna, videlicet Syriæ, in qua pater suus regnavit, et Ægypti, quod nepos ejus habebat.
paras.en: [[1:17|And the kingdom was established|Et paratum est]], that is, disposed to obey, [[1:17|before Antiochus|regnum in conspectu Antiochi]]. For while he was still at Rome, he learned that his father had died; and knowing the sloth of his brother, he left Rome secretly, or (as some say) with the consent of the senators, and came into Syria, and on his brother's death was received as king. [[1:17|and he had a mind to reign over the land of Egypt, that he might reign over two kingdoms|Et cœpit regnare in terra Ægypti, ut regnaret super duo regna]] [*cœpit regnare*, literally 'began to reign'], namely Syria, in which his father had reigned, and Egypt, which his nephew held.

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit quidam: Antiochus, scilicet Magnus, ad confœderationem ipsius cum rege Ægypti, dedit filiam suam Cleopatram Ptolemæo Epiphani, ex quibus natus fuit Ptolemæus Philometor. Ergo mortuo Ptolemæo Epiphane, Antiochus Illustris rex Syriæ accepit aliquas civitates regis Ægypti regno suo propinquas, quasi tutor nepotis sui adhuc pueri: quas quum duces Ægypti repeterent pro puero, et ille nollet reddere, motum fuit bellum inter ipsos et Antiochum, in quo devicti sunt duces Ægypti, et per consequens Ptolemæus Philometor cum eis, adhuc juvenis; et spoliata Ægypto, Antiochus venit Jerosolymam, et fecit ibi mala quæ in textu sequuntur. Hæc ille. Cujus narratio videtur a veritate deficere, quia (ut Josephus et alii referunt) Ptolemæus Philadelphus filiam suam Cleopatram dedit uxorem Antiocho regi Syriæ: quod et Scripturæ concordat canonicæ, quum scriptum sit in Daniele, Filia regis austri veniet ad regem aquilonis facere amicitiam: ubi per regem austri, secundum Hieronymum et ceteros expositores catholicos, intelligitur rex Ægypti, quæ fuit in plaga australi, et sic filia ejus venit ad contrahendum cum Antiocho rege aquilonis, id est Syriæ, quæ fuit versus aquilonem respectu Ægypti.
paras.en: On this a certain writer says: Antiochus, namely the Great, to make a league between himself and the king of Egypt, gave his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemee Epiphanes, of whom was born Ptolemee Philometor. So when Ptolemee Epiphanes died, Antiochus the Illustrious, king of Syria, took certain cities of the king of Egypt that bordered on his own kingdom, as though guardian of his nephew, who was still a boy; and when the captains of Egypt demanded them back for the boy and he would not give them up, war broke out between them and Antiochus, in which the captains of Egypt were defeated, and with them, in consequence, Ptolemee Philometor, still a youth; and when Egypt had been despoiled, Antiochus came to Jerusalem and did there the evils that follow in the text. So far that writer. His account seems to fall short of the truth, because (as Josephus and others relate) Ptolemee Philadelphus gave his daughter Cleopatra as wife to Antiochus king of Syria: which also agrees with canonical Scripture, since it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 11:6|the daughter of the king of the south shall come to the king of the north to make friendship|Filia regis austri veniet ad regem aquilonis facere amicitiam]]; where by the king of the south, according to Jerome and the other Catholic expositors, is understood the king of Egypt, which lay in the southern region; and so his daughter came to contract marriage with Antiochus, king of the north, that is, of Syria, which lay towards the north with respect to Egypt.

paras.t: Itaque Antiochus Illustris ambitione ductus, voluit sibi usurpare regnum Ægypti. Et intravit Ægyptum in multitudine gravi, id est cum exercitu copioso ad sustinendum molesta, in curribus et elephantis, quæ sunt animalia magna, super se ligneas turres gestantia, in quibus sunt bellatores desuper præliantes et jacula emittentes, et equitibus et copiosa navium multitudine. Sicque invasit Ægyptum ex terra et mari, et forsan bello pugnavit contra quosdam Ægyptiorum; et constituit bellum adversus Ptolemæum regem Ægypti, etc. Post Alexandrum Magnum primus in Ægypto regnavit Ptolemæus Lagi filius, qui Ptolemæus cognominatus est Soter: a quo (ut legitur) posteri ejus vocati sunt Ptolemæi, quod fuit eis nomen commune, præter quod habuerunt propria nomina. Quod vero hic dicitur de Ptolemæo, quidam exponunt de Ptolemæo Philometore: quem tamen alii dicunt victum ab Antiocho Magno.
paras.en: And so Antiochus the Illustrious, led by ambition, wished to seize the kingdom of Egypt for himself. [[1:18|And he entered into Egypt with a great multitude|Et intravit Ægyptum in multitudine gravi]], that is, with a numerous army able to bear hardships, [[1:18|with chariots, and elephants|in curribus et elephantis]], which are great animals that carry wooden towers on their backs, in which there are warriors fighting from above and hurling darts, [[1:18|and horsemen, and a great number of ships|et equitibus et copiosa navium multitudine]]. And so he invaded Egypt by land and sea, and perhaps fought in battle against some of the Egyptians; [[1:19|And he made war against Ptolemee king of Egypt|et constituit bellum adversus Ptolemæum regem Ægypti]], etc. After Alexander the Great, the first to reign in Egypt was Ptolemee the son of Lagus, which Ptolemee was surnamed Soter: from whom (as we read) his descendants were called Ptolemees, which was a name common to them, besides the names proper to each. What is said here of Ptolemee, some expound of Ptolemee Philometor: who, however, others say was conquered by Antiochus the Great.

paras.t: Et convertit Antiochus iter suum, et ascendit ad Jerosolymam. Et intravit in sanctificationem, id est in templum Dei sanctificantis, et in quo homines sanctificabantur, cum superbia. Et accepit altare aureum, id est deauratum forinsecus laminis aureis: et exponitur hoc de altari thymiamatis, super quod incendebatur thymiama; eratque in templo, et in exteriore parte ejus, quæ dicitur Sancta; et candelabrum luminis, super quod sitæ erant septem lampades, seu lucernæ aureæ, prout in Exodo jubetur: et universa vasa ejus, id est instrumenta, ut forcipes et emunctoria, quæ secundum Hebræi proprietatem sermonis, vasa vocantur; et mensam propositionis, super quam omni sabbato ponebantur duodecim panes calidi, sublatis inde panibus qui præcedenti sabbato super eam positi erant, prout in Exodo tangitur: et libatoria, quæ erant vasa, in quibus ponebantur materiæ liquidæ, ex quibus fiebant oblationes; et phialas, id est vascula thymiamatum et unguentorum; et mortariola; et velum in medio templi dependens et dividens inter Sancta et Sancta sanctorum, id est exteriorem interioremque partem templi; et coronas insertas quibusdam utensilibus templi; et ornamentum aureum quod in facie templi erat: per quod quidam intelligunt cortinam aurifrigiatam, circa ingressum templi pendentem; et comminuit omnia, id est, a pristina forma frangendo, ad partes minutas redegit, ad faciendum inde aliqua sibi placentia, suoque usui deservientia.
paras.en: And Antiochus [[1:21|returned|Et convertit Antiochus iter suum]], [[1:22|and he went up to Jerusalem|et ascendit ad Jerosolymam]]. And he [[1:23|entered into the sanctuary|Et intravit in sanctificationem]], that is, into the temple of God who sanctifies, in which men were sanctified, [[1:23|proudly|cum superbia]]. [[1:23|and took away the golden altar|Et accepit altare aureum]], that is, gilded on the outside with plates of gold: and this is explained of the altar of incense[[Ex 30:1||]], on which incense was burnt; and it stood in the temple, in the outer part of it, which is called the Holy; [[1:23|and the candlestick of light|et candelabrum luminis]], on which were set seven lamps, or golden lights, as is commanded in Exodus[[Ex 25:31||]][[Ex 25:37||]] [the margin, partly illegible, gives Exod. xxv]: [[1:23|and all the vessels thereof|et universa vasa ejus]], that is, implements, such as tongs and snuffers, which by the idiom of the Hebrew tongue are called vessels; [[1:23|and the table of proposition|et mensam propositionis]], on which every sabbath twelve hot loaves were set, the loaves that had been set on it the sabbath before being taken away, as is touched on in Exodus[[Ex 25:30||]] [the margin is barely legible here; the changing of the loaves every sabbath is in Lev 24:8]; [[1:23|and the pouring vessels|et libatoria]], which were vessels in which liquids were put, of which offerings were made[[Ex 25:29||]]; [[1:23|and the vials|et phialas]], that is, little vessels for incense and ointments; [[1:23|and the little mortars|et mortariola]]; [[1:23|and the veil|et velum]] hanging in the middle of the temple and dividing the Holy from the Holy of holies, that is, the outer from the inner part of the temple; [[1:23|and the crowns|et coronas]] set on certain utensils of the temple; [[1:23|and the golden ornament that was before the temple|et ornamentum aureum quod in facie templi erat]]: by which some understand a curtain worked with gold [*aurifrigiatam*: embroidered with orphrey, gold needlework], hanging about the entrance of the temple; [[1:23|and he broke them all in pieces|et comminuit omnia]], that is, breaking them from their former shape, he reduced them to small pieces, to make from them things pleasing to himself and serving his own use.

paras.t: Denique Ptolemæus Philadelphus, quum ad ejus petitionem Septuaginta interpretes transtulissent vetus Testamentum, misit in templum Jerosolymitanum præter alia aurea vasa, mensam auream gemmis impretiabilibus insignitam, cujus crassitudo, id est spissitudo, quum esset dimidii cubiti, materiam tamen superabat artificii opus. An autem et illam mensam acceperit, quæri potest: et constat, quod sic, si reperit eam. Mensa autem propositionis per Moysen fieri jussa, fuit de lignis setim, ut patet in Exodo. Sed tertio Regum legitur Salomon mensam auream fecisse in templo, quæ jam diu fuit ablata. An vero pretiosissima mensa illa a Ptolemæo missa, fuerat deputata ad mensam propositionis, posset inquiri. Ecce, quid est violentus et impius rex, nisi magnus latro et pessimus fur?
paras.en: Moreover Ptolemee Philadelphus, when at his request the Seventy translators had translated the Old Testament, sent to the temple at Jerusalem, besides other golden vessels, a golden table adorned with priceless gems, whose thickness, that is, depth, was half a cubit; yet the work of the craftsmanship surpassed the material. Whether Antiochus took that table too may be asked: and it is certain that he did, if he found it. Now the table of proposition that Moses was commanded to make was of setim wood, as is plain in Exodus[[Ex 25:23||]]. But in the third book of Kings we read that Solomon made a golden table in the temple[[3 Kings 7:48||]], which had long since been carried off. But whether that most precious table sent by Ptolemee had been appointed to serve as the table of proposition might be inquired. See: what is a violent and wicked king, but a great robber and a very bad thief?

paras.t: Et accepit argentum et aurum in templo reposita et oblata, et vasa concupiscibilia, id est pretiosa et pulchra; et accepit thesauros occultos quos invenit per se et per suos satellites: in quo patet insatiabilis cupiditas ejus, quod tam exquisite perscrutatus est abdita loca, quum tamen in nullo offendissent eum Judæi; et sublatis omnibus, abiit in terram suam. Et fecit cædem hominum, id est, multos occidit: in quo patet sua crudelitas. Et factus est planctus magnus in Israel, id est ab Israelitico populo, præsertim de templi profanatione, et in omni loco eorum, id est in civitatibus et villis Judæorum. Et ingemuerunt principes et seniores, et juvenes et virgines infirmati sunt et tristitia et dolore, et speciositas mulierum immutata est, id est, alterata et versa in discolorationem, et pro vestibus pretiosis induerunt lugubres vestes. Et commota est terra super habitantes in ea, id est, habitantes in terra obstupuerunt propter tot et tanta mala facta in terra Juda. Ipsa quoque terra intuentibus præbuit materiam commotionis propter mala illata habitatoribus terræ. Sed et terra a sua dispositionis decore est alterata, propter tot calamitates inhabitantium eam.
paras.en: [[1:24|And he took the silver and gold|Et accepit argentum et aurum]] laid up and offered in the temple, [[1:24|and the precious vessels|et vasa concupiscibilia]], that is, costly and beautiful [*concupiscibilia*, literally 'desirable']; [[1:24|and he took the hidden treasures, which he found|et accepit thesauros occultos quos invenit]] by himself and by his attendants: in which his insatiable greed is plain, in that he searched out hidden places so carefully, though the Jews had offended him in nothing; [[1:24|and when he had taken all away, he departed into his own country|et sublatis omnibus, abiit in terram suam]]. [[1:25|And he made a great slaughter of men|Et fecit cædem hominum]], that is, he killed many: in which his cruelty is plain. [[1:26|And there was great mourning in Israel|Et factus est planctus magnus in Israel]], that is, by the people of Israel, especially over the profaning of the temple, [[1:26|and in every place where they were|et in omni loco eorum]], that is, in the cities and villages of the Jews. [[1:27|And the princes, and the ancients mourned|Et ingemuerunt principes et seniores]], [[1:27|and the virgins and the young men were made feeble|et juvenes et virgines infirmati sunt]], both with sadness and with grief, [[1:27|and the beauty of the women was changed|et speciositas mulierum immutata est]], that is, altered and turned to discolouring, and in place of costly garments they put on mourning garments. [[1:29|And the land was moved for the inhabitants thereof|Et commota est terra super habitantes in ea]]: that is, the dwellers in the land were struck with amazement at so many and such great evils done in the land of Juda. The land itself, too, gave those who beheld it matter for being moved, because of the evils brought on the dwellers in the land. And the land, too, was altered from the beauty of its order because of the many calamities of those who dwelt in it.

paras.t: Et post duos annos dierum. Cur, quum dixisset, Annos, addidit, Dierum? Forsan quia sicut in lege erant hebdomades dierum, hebdomadesque annorum, quarum quilibet continuit septem annos, ita de annis. Misit rex principem tributorum, id est superiorem inter eos qui tributa levabant pro rege, et venit Jerusalem cum turba magna. Et locutus est ad eos, id est ad habitatores Jerusalem, verba pacifica in dolo, dicendo se venisse pro utilitate ipsorum; et crediderunt ei. Et irruit super civitatem repente, id est, statim quum fuerat intromissus, et percussit eam plaga, et perdidit, id est occidit, populum multum. Et succendit eam, scilicet urbem Jerusalem pro parte, non totam; et destruxit domos ejus validiores, ex quibus potuissent Judæi resistere hostibus suis, et muros ejus in circuitu, non dejiciendo muros totaliter, sed faciendo in muris hinc inde interruptiones et aperturas, per quas pateret eis ingressus in urbem dum vellent.
paras.en: [[1:30|And after two full years|Et post duos annos dierum]] [literally 'after two years of days']. Why, when he had said *years*, did he add *of days*? Perhaps because, as in the law there were weeks of days and weeks of years[[Lev 25:8||]], each of the latter holding seven years, so it is with years. [[1:30|the king sent the chief collector of his tributes|Misit rex principem tributorum]], that is, the superior among those who levied tributes for the king, [[1:30|and he came to Jerusalem with a great multitude|et venit Jerusalem cum turba magna]]. [[1:31|And he spoke to them|Et locutus est ad eos]], that is, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, [[1:31|peaceable words in deceit|verba pacifica in dolo]], saying that he had come for their good; [[1:31|and they believed him|et crediderunt ei]]. [[1:32|And he fell upon the city suddenly|Et irruit super civitatem repente]], that is, as soon as he had been let in, [[1:32|and struck it with a great slaughter|et percussit eam plaga]], [[1:32|and destroyed|et perdidit]], that is, killed, [[1:32|much people|populum multum]]. [[1:33|and burnt it with fire|Et succendit eam]], namely the city of Jerusalem, in part, not the whole; [[1:33|and threw down the houses thereof|et destruxit domos ejus]], the stronger ones, from which the Jews could have resisted their enemies, [[1:33|and the walls thereof round about|et muros ejus in circuitu]]: not throwing the walls down wholly, but making breaches and openings in the walls here and there, through which there might be entry into the city for them when they wished.

paras.t: Et ædificaverunt civitatem David, id est arcem illam in sublimitate montis Sion, ubi David aliquando habitavit, muro magno et firmo in gyro, vel muris fortibus loco parietum, et turribus firmis, ex quibus possent ejicere jacula; et facta est illis in arcem, id est, pro castro et fortalitio usi sunt ea. Et posuerunt illic gentem peccatricem; et facti sunt in laqueum magnum, id est, impii habitantes in arce, usi sunt ipsa arce tanquam laqueo, ad capiendum affligendumque Judæos in Jerusalem commorantes. Et factum est hoc ad insidias sanctificationi, id est templo, ut scilicet ex arce impedirent Judæos a templi ingressu, quod fuit juxta arcem, ejiciendo jacula super intrantes templum, et in diabolum malum, vel, ut aliqui habent, in diabolicum, id est maximum malum, in Israel: quia fuit destructivum cultus divini ac boni communis. Et contaminaverunt sanctificationem, id est, templum violaverunt.
paras.en: [[1:35|And they built the city of David|Et ædificaverunt civitatem David]], that is, that citadel on the height of mount Sion where David once dwelt[[2 Kings 5:9||]], [[1:35|with a great and strong wall|muro magno et firmo]] round about, or with strong walls in place of house walls, [[1:35|and with strong towers|et turribus firmis]], from which they could hurl darts; [[1:35|and made it a fortress for them|et facta est illis in arcem]], that is, they used it as a castle and stronghold. [[1:36|And they placed there a sinful nation|Et posuerunt illic gentem peccatricem]]; [[1:37|and they became a great snare|et facti sunt in laqueum magnum]]: that is, the wicked who dwelt in the citadel used the citadel itself as a snare to catch and afflict the Jews living in Jerusalem. [[1:38|And this was a place to lie in wait against the sanctuary|Et factum est hoc ad insidias sanctificationi]], that is, against the temple: namely, that from the citadel they might hinder the Jews from entering the temple, which was next to the citadel, by hurling darts on those going into the temple; [[1:38|and an evil devil|et in diabolum malum]], or, as some have it, *a devilish thing*, that is, a very great evil, [[1:38|in Israel|in Israel]]: because it was destructive of divine worship and of the common good. [[1:39|and defiled the holy place|Et contaminaverunt sanctificationem]], that is, they violated the temple.

paras.t: Et facta est Jerusalem habitatio exterorum, id est extraneorum: ex quo patet quod non fuit tota destructa; et facta est extera semini suo, hoc est aliena a propriis civibus inibi natis. Sanctificatio ejus desolata est sicut solitudo, id est, templum destitutum est, et privatum suo honore, cultu ac ministrorum frequentia; dies festi ejus conversi sunt in luctum, id est, pro gaudiis solennitatum, successerunt lamenta. Secundum gloriam ejus, multiplicata est ignominia ejus: id est, quo major fuit apparatus templi in cultu, honore et gaudio temporibus pristinis prosperitatis, etiam Antiochi Magni, ut habetur libro secundo, eo sub impiissimo isto Antiocho major facta ejus inhonoratio.
paras.en: [[1:40|and the city was made the habitation of strangers|Et facta est Jerusalem habitatio exterorum]], that is, of foreigners: from which it is plain that it was not wholly destroyed; [[1:40|and she became a stranger to her own seed|et facta est extera semini suo]], that is, foreign to her own citizens born there. [[1:41|Her sanctuary was desolate like a wilderness|Sanctificatio ejus desolata est sicut solitudo]]: that is, the temple was forsaken and deprived of its honour, its worship and the throng of its ministers; [[1:41|her festival days were turned into mourning|dies festi ejus conversi sunt in luctum]], that is, in place of the joys of the solemn feasts came lamentations. [[1:42|Her dishonour was increased according to her glory|Secundum gloriam ejus, multiplicata est ignominia ejus]]: that is, the greater the splendour of the temple had been in worship, honour and joy in the former times of prosperity, even under Antiochus the Great, as we have it in the second book, the greater was its dishonouring under this most wicked Antiochus.

paras.t: His objici potest, quia (ut Josephus refert duodecimo libro Antiquitatum, et Magister in historiis) quum Antiochus redisset in Ægyptum, et inde esset repulsus per Romanorum legatos, quibus Ægyptii tunc erant confœderati, post biennium rediit in Jerusalem cum furore, et fecit in ea quæ jam recitata sunt hic, et alia plura: ergo personaliter venit, nec per principem tributorum commisit hæc scelera, præsertim quum infra secundi libri capitulo quinto conscriptum sit, Eodem tempore Antiochus secundam profectionem paravit in Ægyptum. Et sicut in expositione illius capituli dicunt Rabanus, Glossa et alii expositores, Antiochus ab Ægypto tunc rediens effrenatis animis venit Jerusalem. Ad istud videtur dicendum, scripturam istam, videlicet hujus primi capituli, non loqui de reditu illo Antiochi in Jerusalem, sed de adventu prætacti principis tributorum, missi ab Antiocho paulo post quum recessisset Antiochus a civitate Jerusalem conculcata: de quo adventu præallegato secundi libri capitulo quinto habetur: Misit odiosum principem Apollonium cum exercitu viginti et duobus millibus, præcipiens eis, omnes perfectæ ætatis interficere. Quod autem princeps ille verba pacifica loquebatur in dolo, tangitur ibi his verbis: Qui quum venisset Jerosolymam, pacem simulans, quievit usque ad diem sanctum sabbati.
paras.en: Against these things it may be objected that (as Josephus relates in the twelfth book of the Antiquities, and the Master in the Histories) when Antiochus had gone back into Egypt and had been driven from there by the legates of the Romans, with whom the Egyptians were then in league, after two years he returned to Jerusalem in fury and did in it what has been recounted here, and much else besides: therefore he came in person, and did not commit these crimes through the chief collector of tributes; especially since it is written below, in the fifth chapter of the second book: [[2 Mach 5:1|At the same time Antiochus prepared for a second journey into Egypt.|Eodem tempore Antiochus secundam profectionem paravit in Ægyptum]] And, as Rabanus, the Gloss and other expositors say in expounding that chapter, Antiochus, returning then from Egypt, came to Jerusalem with unbridled spirit. To this it seems we must say that this scripture, namely of this first chapter, does not speak of that return of Antiochus to Jerusalem, but of the coming of the aforesaid chief collector of tributes, sent by Antiochus a little after Antiochus had left the city of Jerusalem, which he had trodden underfoot: of which coming we have in the fifth chapter of the second book, cited above: [[2 Mach 5:24|he sent that hateful prince, Apollonius, with an army of two and twenty thousand men, commanding him to kill all that were of perfect age|Misit odiosum principem Apollonium cum exercitu viginti et duobus millibus, præcipiens eis, omnes perfectæ ætatis interficere]]. And that this prince spoke peaceable words in deceit is touched on there in these words: [[2 Mach 5:25|Who, when he was come to Jerusalem, pretending peace, rested till the holy day of the sabbath|Qui quum venisset Jerosolymam, pacem simulans, quievit usque ad diem sanctum sabbati]].

paras.t: Et scripsit Antiochus omni regno suo, id est cunctis regionibus sibi subjectis, inter quas fuit tunc terra Judæorum, regibus Syriæ subdita, ut essent omnes populus unus, id est unius observantiæ et culturæ seu legis ac ritus. Unitas enim populi, ex unitate legis et observantiæ cerimonialium perpenditur; similiter ex unitate capitis seu prælati. Ad quod insinuandum ait Salvator: Fiet unus pastor et unum ovile. Hinc in Genesi Hemor et Sichem dixisse leguntur: Si circumcidamus masculos nostros, ritum gentis sequentes, unus efficiemur populus. Et reliquerunt unusquisque legem suam, id est quilibet subditorum Antiochi, qui aliam legem habuit ante, quam ipse. Et consenserunt omnes gentes, quæ erant sub ditione Antiochi, ejus edicto: non tamen simpliciter omnes, potissime in Judæa, ut infra habetur. Et multi ex Israel consenserunt præcepto tyranni illius prætacto, et sacrificaverunt idolis, et coinquinaverunt, id est, transgressi sunt, sabbatum, faciendo in eo servilia opera.
paras.en: [[1:43|And king Antiochus wrote to all his kingdom|Et scripsit Antiochus omni regno suo]], that is, to all the regions subject to him, among which was then the land of the Jews, subject to the kings of Syria, [[1:43|that all the people should be one|ut essent omnes populus unus]], that is, of one observance and worship, or of one law and rite. For the unity of a people is weighed by the unity of its law and of its ceremonial observance; and likewise by the unity of its head or prelate. To hint at this the Saviour says: [[John 10:16|there shall be one fold and one shepherd|Fiet unus pastor et unum ovile]]. Hence in Genesis Hemor and Sichem are read to have said: [[Gen 34:22|We must circumcise every male among us, following the manner of the nation|Si circumcidamus masculos nostros, ritum gentis sequentes]], [[Gen 34:23|we shall make one people|unus efficiemur populus]]. [[1:43|and every one should leave his own law|Et reliquerunt unusquisque legem suam]], that is, each of the subjects of Antiochus who had before a law other than his. [[1:44|And all nations consented|Et consenserunt omnes gentes]] that were under the rule of Antiochus, to his edict: yet not all without exception, above all in Judea, as is told below. [[1:45|And many of Israel consented|Et multi ex Israel consenserunt]] to the aforesaid command of that tyrant, [[1:45|and they sacrificed to idols|et sacrificaverunt idolis]], [[1:45|and profaned|et coinquinaverunt]], that is, transgressed, [[1:45|the sabbath|sabbatum]], by doing servile works on it.

paras.t: Et misit Antiochus libros, id est epistolas decretales, in Jerusalem, ut sequerentur leges gentium terræ, hoc est instituta idololatrarum regni sui, et prohiberent vel nuntii Antiochi, vel majores Judæorum, holocausta et sacrificia et placationes fieri in templo Dei. Per holocausta intelliguntur oblationes quæ ad divinæ reverentiam majestatis totaliter comburebantur, in signum quod rationalis creatura debeat se omnino sui Creatoris obsequiis mancipare, et ejus amore succendi. Per sacrificia vero, hoc loco intelliguntur oblationes pacificæ atque spontaneæ; per placationes autem, hostiæ pro peccato, quibus Dominus placabatur. Et coinquinari sancta et sanctum populum Israel. Hoc refertur non ad verbum illud, Ut prohiberent, sed ad illud, Misit ut sequerentur, etc. Et coinquinari sancta, id est loca sacra, ut templum et synagogas, sacramentaque legis, et populum Israeliticum ad veri Dei cultum electum, vitiis gentilitatis fœdari. Et jussit ædificari aras, id est altaria, super quæ sacrificaretur diis et idolis suis, et templa, id est fana deorum, et immolari carnes suillas, id est porcinas, et pecora communia, hoc est immunda et lege prohibita; et ut immutarent omnes justificationes Dei, id est, observantias omnium præceptorum Dei, per quas homo fit justus, omitterent, atque pro eis observantias gentilitatis assumerent.
paras.en: [[1:46|And the king sent letters|Et misit Antiochus libros]] [*libros*, literally 'books'], that is, letters of decree, [[1:46|to Jerusalem|in Jerusalem]], [[1:46|that they should follow the law of the nations of the earth|ut sequerentur leges gentium terræ]], that is, the institutions of the idolaters of his kingdom; [[1:47|And should forbid|et prohiberent]], whether the messengers of Antiochus or the elders of the Jews, [[1:47|holocausts and sacrifices, and atonements to be made in the temple of God|holocausta et sacrificia et placationes fieri in templo Dei]]. By holocausts are meant the offerings that were wholly burnt in reverence of the divine majesty, in sign that the rational creature ought to give itself up wholly to the service of its Creator, and be set on fire with his love. By sacrifices, in this place, are meant peace offerings and freewill offerings; and by atonements, the victims for sin by which the Lord was appeased. [[1:49|the holy places to be profaned, and the holy people of Israel|Et coinquinari sancta et sanctum populum Israel]]. This is referred not to the words *that they should forbid*, but to *he sent … that they should follow*, etc. [[1:49|the holy places to be profaned|Et coinquinari sancta]]: that is, that the sacred places, such as the temple and the synagogues, and the sacraments of the law, and the people of Israel chosen for the worship of the true God, should be fouled with the vices of heathenism. [[1:50|And he commanded altars to be built|Et jussit ædificari aras]], that is, altars on which sacrifice might be made to his gods and idols, [[1:50|and temples|et templa]], that is, shrines of the gods, [[1:50|and swine's flesh to be immolated|et immolari carnes suillas]], that is, pork, [[1:50|and unclean beasts|et pecora communia]] [*communia*, literally 'common'], that is, beasts unclean and forbidden by the law; [[1:51|and should change all the justifications of God|et ut immutarent omnes justificationes Dei]]: that is, that they should leave off the observances of all the precepts of God, by which man becomes just, and take up instead the observances of heathenism.

paras.t: Et congregati sunt multi de populo Israel ad eos, qui dereliquerant legem Domini, hoc est ad impiissimos illos Judæos, qui ante hanc Antiochi jussionem assumpserunt ritum gentilium, sicut præhabitum est, ut fuerunt Jason et Menelaus cum suis fautoribus; et effugaverunt populum Israel, non acquiescentem eis, in abditis, id est ad speluncas, ad quas ex timore fugerunt.
paras.en: [[1:55|Then many of the people were gathered to them that had forsaken the law of the Lord|Et congregati sunt multi de populo Israel ad eos, qui dereliquerant legem Domini]], that is, to those most wicked Jews who before this command of Antiochus had taken up the rite of the Gentiles, as was said before, such as Jason and Menelaus with their supporters; [[1:56|And they drove away the people of Israel|et effugaverunt populum Israel]], who would not go along with them, [[1:56|into lurking holes|in abditis]], that is, to caves, to which they fled out of fear.

paras.t: Die quintadecima mensis Casleu, qui correspondet nostro Decembri, quamvis interdum concurrat cum Novembri, sicut antiqui Catholici, Beda, Haymo, Rabanus, Magister in historiis, et alii doctissimi, qui cum Hebræis sæpissime contulerunt, bene scripserunt: quamvis quidam posterorum, de hoc reprehendere illos frequenter adjecerit. Ædificavit Antiochus abominandum idolum desolationis, id est idolum Jovis, sicut secundo libro plenius recitatur: quod fuit causa desolationis fidelium Judæorum, et signum desolationis templi.
paras.en: [[1:57|On the fifteenth day of the month, Casleu|Die quintadecima mensis Casleu]], which corresponds to our December, though at times it falls together with November, as the ancient Catholic writers, Bede, Haymo, Rabanus, the Master in the Histories and other most learned men, who very often conferred with the Hebrews, rightly wrote; although one of the later writers has often gone on to find fault with them on this point. [[1:57|king Antiochus set up the abominable idol of desolation|Ædificavit Antiochus abominandum idolum desolationis]], that is, the idol of Jupiter, as is told more fully in the second book[[2 Mach 6:2||]]: which was the cause of the desolation of the faithful Jews and the sign of the desolation of the temple.

paras.t: Et libros legis Dei, videlicet libros Moysis, et alios etiam libros veteris Testamenti, ut reor, combusserunt: sicut Chaldæi ante fecerunt. In virtute sua, id est potestate tyrannica, faciebant hæc populo Israel. Et sacrificabant idolo Jovis, super aram quæ erat contra altare, id est ex opposito altaris Dei. Sicut enim ædificavit in templo idolum illud turpissimum, sic et aram ejusdem. Et suspendebant pueros, id est infantulos circumcisos, a cervicibus, id est in collis per funes euntes juxta cervices. Verumtamen secundo libro leguntur duæ mulieres, quæ circumciderant parvulos suos, fuisse præcipitatæ, infantibus ad ubera suspensis.
paras.en: And [[1:59|the books of the law of God|Et libros legis Dei]], namely the books of Moses, and also, as I think, the other books of the Old Testament, they [[1:59|burnt|combusserunt]]: as the Chaldeans had done before[[2 Par 36:19||]]. [[1:61|Thus by their power|In virtute sua]], that is, by tyrannical might, [[1:61|did they deal with the people of Israel|faciebant hæc populo Israel]]. And [[1:62|they sacrificed|Et sacrificabant]] to the idol of Jupiter, [[1:62|upon the altar of the idol that was over against the altar of God|super aram quæ erat contra altare]], that is, facing the altar of God. For as he built that most foul idol in the temple, so too he built its altar. [[1:64|And they hanged the children|Et suspendebant pueros]], that is, the circumcised little ones, [[1:64|about their neck|a cervicibus]], that is, on the necks, by cords passing round the neck. However, in the second book we read that two women who had circumcised their little ones were thrown down headlong, [[2 Mach 6:10|with the infants hanging at their breasts|infantibus ad ubera suspensis]].

2.title: Expositio capituli secundi: In diebus illis surrexit Mathathias filius Joannis.
2.title_en: Exposition of the second chapter: In those days arose Mathathias, the son of John.

paras.t: Recitata Judæorum tribulatione acerrima, describitur hic exordium subventionis eorum. In diebus illis surrexit, id est, ad gesta virilia se erexit, Mathathias filius Joannis, filii Simeonis, sacerdos ex filiis Joarim: qui Joarim fuit unus viginti quatuor sacerdotum post pontificem principalium, quos primo libro Paralipomenon David legitur instituisse. Verumtamen iste nominatur ibi alio nomine. Nam et infra Joarim iste vocatur Jarib. Surrexit, inquam, et abiit a Jerusalem, ubi ministravit in templo. Sic et Zacharias pater beatissimi Joannis Baptistæ dicitur fuisse de vice Abia. Et consedit in monte Modin, id est in oppido situato in loco montuoso, quod Modin vocatur.
paras.en: After the most bitter tribulation of the Jews has been recounted, the beginning of their relief is described here. [[2:1|In those days arose|In diebus illis surrexit]], that is, roused himself to manly deeds, [[2:1|Mathathias, the son of John, the son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib|Mathathias filius Joannis, filii Simeonis, sacerdos ex filiis Joarim]] [Denis's text reads *Joarim* here and below; a footnote in the edition gives the other reading, *Joarib*, which the Douay-Rheims follows]: this Joarim was one of the twenty-four principal priests after the high priest, whom David is read in the first book of Paralipomenon to have instituted[[1 Par 24:1||]]. But this man is named there by another name[[1 Par 24:7||]] [that is, *Jojarib*, to whom the first lot fell]. For further on, too, this Joarim is called Jarib[[1 Mach 14:29||]]. He arose, I say, and went away [[2:1|from Jerusalem|a Jerusalem]], where he ministered in the temple. So too Zachary, the father of the most blessed John the Baptist, is said to have been [[Luke 1:5|of the course of Abia|de vice Abia]] [that is, of another of those twenty-four courses of priests]. [[2:1|And he abode in the mountain of Modin|Et consedit in monte Modin]], that is, in a town set in a mountainous place, which is called Modin.

paras.t: Et habebat filios quinque, quorum nomina et cognomina ponuntur in littera: et sicut virtus consistit in medio, sic medius inter illos fuit Judas Machabæus, virtuosissimus et strenuissimus inter fratres suos. Hi viderunt oculo exteriori et interiori mala quæ fiebant, etc.
paras.en: [[2:2|And he had five sons|Et habebat filios quinque]], whose names and surnames are set down in the text; and as virtue stands in the mean, so in the middle of them was Judas Machabeus, the most virtuous and the most vigorous among his brothers. [[2:6|These saw|Hi viderunt]] with the outward and the inward eye [[2:6|the evils that were done|mala quæ fiebant]], etc.

paras.t: Et dixit Mathathias: Væ mihi, temporalis tristitiæ et doloris. Juxta quem modum loquitur Michæas: Væ mihi, quia factus sum sicut homo qui colligit in autumno racemos vindemiæ. Ut quid natus sum videre contritionem, id est destructionem et desolationem, populi mei, de quo natus sum, et contritionem civitatis sanctæ Jerusalem, quæ fuit specialiter ad Dei cultum electa, et sedere illic, id est, ibi esse ad faciendum sacerdotale officium, si esset possibile? Circa hæc verba, Væ mihi, ut quid natus sum videre, etc., quidam scribit: Quasi diceret, Minus malum mihi esset, simpliciter non esse, quam tanta populi mala et contemptum cultus divini videre. Quod non videtur idonee dictum. Nam quamvis minus malum sit, non esse simpliciter quam peccare, non tamen minus malum est, non esse simpliciter quam videre mala quæcumque pœnæ et culpæ, præsertim dum videntur cum compassione, displicentia, aut mentis renisu, prout Mathathias hic ea vidit.
paras.en: [[2:7|And Mathathias said: Woe is me|Et dixit Mathathias: Væ mihi]]: a woe of temporal sorrow and grief. In the same manner Micheas speaks: [[Mich 7:1|Woe is me, for I am become as one that gleaneth in autumn the grapes of the vintage|Væ mihi, quia factus sum sicut homo qui colligit in autumno racemos vindemiæ]]. [[2:7|wherefore was I born to see the ruin|Ut quid natus sum videre contritionem]], that is, the destruction and desolation, [[2:7|of my people|populi mei]], of whom I was born, [[2:7|and the ruin of the holy city|et contritionem civitatis sanctæ]] Jerusalem, which was specially chosen for the worship of God, [[2:7|and to dwell there|et sedere illic]], that is, to be there to perform the priestly office, if that were possible? On these words, [[2:7|Woe is me, wherefore was I born to see|Væ mihi, ut quid natus sum videre]], etc., someone writes: As if he said, It would be a lesser evil for me simply not to be, than to see such great evils of the people and contempt of divine worship. This does not seem fitly said. For although it is a lesser evil simply not to be than to sin, yet it is not a lesser evil simply not to be than to see any evils whatever of punishment and of guilt [the schools distinguish the evil of punishment, which is suffered, from the evil of guilt, which is sin], especially when they are seen with compassion, displeasure, or the mind's resistance, as Mathathias saw them here.

paras.t: Quum datur in manibus inimicorum. Sancta in manu extraneorum facta sunt, id est, sacra loca et vasa templi gentibus tradita sunt; templum ejus contemptum est, et vilibus usibus mancipatum, sicut homo ignobilis. Quæ gens non hæreditavit regnum ejus? quasi dicat: Valde diversæ nationes obtinuerunt successive Judæam, videlicet Assyrii, Chaldæi, Syri et gentes eis admixtæ.
paras.en: [[2:7|when it is given into the hands of the enemies?|Quum datur in manibus inimicorum]] [[2:8|The holy places are come into the hands of strangers|Sancta in manu extraneorum facta sunt]], that is, the sacred places and the vessels of the temple have been handed over to the Gentiles; [[2:8|her temple|templum ejus]] has been held in contempt and given over to base uses, [[2:8|as a man without honour|sicut homo ignobilis]]. [[2:10|What nation hath not inherited her kingdom|Quæ gens non hæreditavit regnum ejus]]? As if to say: very different nations have held Judæa one after another, namely the Assyrians, the Chaldeans, the Syrians, and the peoples mixed with them.

paras.t: Omnis compositio ejus, id est decor seu venustas, ablata est. Quæ erat libera, facta est ancilla: id est, Synagoga seu gens Judæorum, quæ consuevit soli Deo esse subjecta, et ab humanæ servitutis oppressionisque jugo immunis, facta est gentilibus serviens sub tributo ac jugo gravissimo. Sic et Jeremias ait in Threnis: Facta est quasi vidua domina gentium; princeps provinciarum facta est sub tributo.
paras.en: [[2:11|All her ornaments|Omnis compositio ejus]], that is, her comeliness or beauty, [[2:11|are taken away|ablata est]]. [[2:11|She that was free is made a slave|Quæ erat libera, facta est ancilla]]: that is, the Synagogue or nation of the Jews, which was wont to be subject to God alone, and free from the yoke of human servitude and oppression, has been made to serve the Gentiles under tribute and a most heavy yoke. So too Jeremias says in the Lamentations: [[Lam 1:1|how is the mistress of the Gentiles become as a widow: the princes of provinces made tributary!|Facta est quasi vidua domina gentium; princeps provinciarum facta est sub tributo]]

paras.t: Et ecce sancta nostra, id est sacra observantia legis, et pulchritudo nostra, id est templi ac plebis venustas, et claritas nostra, id est nobilitas veræ libertatis, consistens in solius Dei obsequio, desolata est, et coinquinaverunt, id est corruperunt seu inhonoraverunt, ea gentes. Quo ergo nobis adhuc vivere? Id est, potius optare debemus, seu tolerabilius nobis esse debet bene mori, quam tot et talia mala conspicere. Unde quarto libro Regum Dominus ait Josiæ: Colligam te ad patres tuos, ut non videant oculi tui omnia mala quæ inducturus sum super locum istum.
paras.en: [[2:12|And behold our sanctuary|Et ecce sancta nostra]], that is, the sacred observance of the law, [[2:12|and our beauty|et pulchritudo nostra]], that is, the comeliness of the temple and of the people, [[2:12|and our glory|et claritas nostra]], that is, the nobility of true freedom, which consists in the service of God alone, [[2:12|is laid waste|desolata est]], [[2:12|and the Gentiles have defiled|et coinquinaverunt]], that is, corrupted or dishonoured, [[2:12|them|ea gentes]]. [[2:13|To what end then should we live any longer?|Quo ergo nobis adhuc vivere]] That is, we ought rather to wish, or it ought to be more bearable to us, to die well than to behold so many and such evils. Hence in the fourth book of Kings the Lord says to Josias: [[4 Kings 22:20|I will gather thee to thy fathers|Colligam te ad patres tuos]], [[4 Kings 22:20|that thy eyes may not see all the evils which I will bring upon this place|ut non videant oculi tui omnia mala quæ inducturus sum super locum istum]].

paras.t: Et scidit Mathathias et filii ejus vestimenta sua, sicut moris fuit Judæis, et item quibusdam gentilibus in magnis adversis, in signum mœroris; et operuerunt, id est induerunt, se ciliciis, affligendo corpus suum ad impetrandum misericordiam Dei: planxeruntque valde ex dolore de calamitatibus tantis, præsertim de dissipatione divini cultus.
paras.en: [[2:14|And Mathathias and his sons rent their garments|Et scidit Mathathias et filii ejus vestimenta sua]], as was the custom of the Jews, and likewise of some Gentiles, in great adversities, in sign of grief; [[2:14|and they covered|et operuerunt]], that is, clothed, [[2:14|themselves with haircloth|se ciliciis]], afflicting their bodies to obtain the mercy of God: [[2:14|and made great lamentation|planxeruntque valde]] out of grief over calamities so great, and above all over the scattering of the worship of God.

paras.t: Et venerunt illuc missi a rege, ut cogerent eos qui confugerant in civitatem Modin, immolare diis et accendere thura ad honorem eorum, et a lege Dei discedere, etc. Et respondit Mathathias, et dixit magna voce: Ego et filii et fratres mei, id est cognati sive germani, obediemus legi, imo et auctori datorique legis, patrum nostrorum, etc.
paras.en: [[2:15|And they that were sent from king Antiochus, came thither|Et venerunt illuc missi a rege]], [[2:15|to compel them that were fled into the city of Modin, to sacrifice|ut cogerent eos qui confugerant in civitatem Modin, immolare]] to the gods, [[2:15|and to burn incense|et accendere thura]] in their honour, [[2:15|and to depart from the law of God|et a lege Dei discedere]], etc. [[2:19|Then Mathathias answered, and said with a loud voice|Et respondit Mathathias, et dixit magna voce]]: [[2:20|I and my sons, and my brethren|Ego et filii et fratres mei]], that is, kinsmen or brothers by blood, [[2:20|will obey the law|obediemus legi]] (nay, and the Author and Giver of the law) [[2:20|of our fathers|patrum nostrorum]], etc.

paras.t: Et vidit Mathathias Judæum quemdam accedentem ad sacrificandum, et doluit de tanto facinore, præsertim quoniam erat scandalizativum omnium adstantium Judæorum; et contremuerunt renes ejus, ex redundantia vehementium affectionum animæ sensitivæque partis in corpus, juxta illud Isaiæ: Corrui quum audirem, conturbatus sum quum viderem; emarcuit cor meum. Et accensus est furor ejus, id est, ira ejus per zelum inflammata est, secundum judicium legis, hoc est, sicut lex dictat, et vera requirit discretio: quoniam ira illa sic regulata, cooperatur ad exsequendum actum justitiæ, secundum Philosophum; et insiliens trucidavit eum, scilicet Judæum illum idolo sacrificantem, super aram: quemadmodum Phinees perfodit Zambri Judæum, cum Cozbi Madianitide se commiscentem, prout in Numeris narratur.
paras.en: [[2:24|And Mathathias saw|Et vidit Mathathias]] [[2:23|a certain Jew|Judæum quemdam]] coming forward to sacrifice, [[2:24|and was grieved|et doluit]] at so great a crime, especially since it was a cause of scandal to all the Jews standing by; [[2:24|and his reins trembled|et contremuerunt renes ejus]], from the overflowing of the vehement affections of the soul and of its sensitive part into the body, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 21:3|I fell down at the hearing of it, I was troubled at the seeing of it|Corrui quum audirem, conturbatus sum quum viderem]]; [[Is 21:4|My heart failed|emarcuit cor meum]]. And [[2:24|his wrath was kindled|accensus est furor ejus]], that is, his anger was inflamed through zeal, [[2:24|according to the judgment of the law|secundum judicium legis]], that is, as the law dictates and true discretion requires: for anger so regulated works together toward carrying out an act of justice, according to the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle]; [[2:24|and running upon him he slew him|et insiliens trucidavit eum]], namely that Jew sacrificing to the idol, [[2:24|upon the altar|super aram]]: as Phinees thrust through Zambri, a Jew, as he lay with Cozbi the Madianite, as is told in Numbers[[Num 25:8||]].

paras.t: Sed et virum qui cogebat immolare idolo, occidit, tanquam hostem reipublicæ, ac violentatorem ad recedendum a cultu Dei: imo secundum Josephum, Mathathias cum filiis suis, occidit virum illum cum militibus secum missis, qui pauci fuerunt. In Scholastica quoque fertur historia: Surgens Mathathias, trucidavit eum, scilicet præfatum Judæum, et nuntios regis interemit. Et zelatus est legem, id est, cum fervore eam dilexit, sicut opere demonstravit: quemadmodum ait Elias, Zelo zelatus sum pro Domino exercituum.
paras.en: [[2:25|Moreover the man|Sed et virum]] [[2:25|who compelled them to sacrifice|qui cogebat immolare]] to the idol, [[2:25|he slew|occidit]], as an enemy of the commonwealth, and one who used violence to make men forsake the worship of God: nay, according to Josephus, Mathathias with his sons slew that man together with the soldiers sent with him, who were few. In the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor] too it is related: Mathathias, rising up, slew him, that is, the aforesaid Jew, and killed the king's messengers. [[2:26|And shewed zeal for the law|Et zelatus est legem]], that is, loved it with fervour, as he showed by deed: as Elias says, [[3 Kings 19:10|With zeal have I been zealous for the Lord God of hosts|Zelo zelatus sum pro Domino exercituum]][[3 Kings 19:14||]].

paras.t: Et exclamavit: Omnis qui zelum habet legis divinæ datæ per Moysen, statuens testamentum, id est, firmiter proponens vetus Testamentum servare, exeat post me. Et fugit ipse et filii ejus in montes, id est ad loca montana deserti.
paras.en: [[2:27|And Mathathias cried out|Et exclamavit]]: [[2:27|Every one that hath zeal for the law|Omnis qui zelum habet legis]] of God given through Moses, [[2:27|and maintaineth the testament|statuens testamentum]], that is, firmly purposing to keep the Old Testament, [[2:27|let him follow me|exeat post me]]. [[2:28|So he and his sons fled into the mountains|Et fugit ipse et filii ejus in montes]], that is, to the mountain places of the desert.
